<reflection>
After two experiments, the fitting results show a cluster of models with very similar NLL values, led by M16, M11, M13, M19, M14, M20, M9, M18, and M7. The differences among them are small, indicating that the data so far does not strongly discriminate between these mechanisms. The aim of the second experiment (adding product) was to test for product-induced deactivation (M17), but M17 remains in the middle of the pack, suggesting that product deactivation is not a dominant feature. Therefore, we need a new experiment that targets the differences among the top candidates, particularly focusing on the nature of deactivation (first-order vs. second-order, substrate-involved vs. catalyst-involved) and the presence of reversible substrate inhibition (M7).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
The leading candidates involve various deactivation pathways or substrate inhibition. A key discriminative feature is the order of deactivation with respect to catalyst concentration. Models like M13 (2cat→inactive), M18 (2catS→inactive), and M19 (cat+catS→inactive) involve second-order steps that will be strongly amplified at high catalyst concentrations. In contrast, first-order deactivation models (M9, M14, M20) and substrate-involved deactivation (M11, M16) may show less dramatic dependence on catalyst concentration. Additionally, M7 (reversible substrate inhibition) does not involve irreversible deactivation but may show a slowdown due to equilibrium partitioning into catS2. By running an experiment with high catalyst concentration (0.15 M) and moderate substrate (1.0 M), we can observe whether the reaction exhibits rapid deactivation consistent with second-order processes. Predictions: For M13, the high catalyst concentration will cause rapid loss of active catalyst via dimerization, leading to a sharp early plateau in product formation. For M18 and M19, similar rapid deactivation is expected, though the exact shape may differ. For first-order deactivation models (M9, M14), the deactivation rate will be proportional to catalyst concentration only indirectly (through catS for M14), so the progress curve may show a more gradual decay. For M7, no irreversible deactivation occurs; the curve will approach equilibrium smoothly, possibly with a slower effective rate due to substrate inhibition but no premature plateau. This experiment should separate second-order deactivation models from first-order ones and from reversible inhibition.
</hypothesis>
